canonical_statement: The network meta-analysis aimed to compare cardiovascular, metabolic, renal, and safety treatment effects between SGLT2 inhibitors and combined SGLT1/2 inhibitors in patients with diabetes.

Eligible studies were randomized controlled trials in patients with diabetes evaluating an SGLT2 inhibitor or combined SGLT1/2 inhibitor for at least 12 weeks and reporting cardiovascular, metabolic, renal, or safety outcomes.

canonical_statement: PubMed, Embase, Cochrane, and Scopus were searched from inception through 15 January 2022.
Four reviewers independently performed the literature search and data extraction, with disagreements resolved by consensus.
Risk of bias was assessed by two independent reviewers using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool.
The quality of pooled network evidence was evaluated using a modified GRADE approach accounting for inconsistency, publication bias, risk of bias, indirectness, and imprecision.

Frequentist network meta-analysis of aggregate data was performed in Stata 16.0; transitivity/consistency was assessed with a global Wald test, using consistency models when p>0.10 and inconsistency models when p<0.10.
Treatment effects were reported as hazard ratios or risk ratios for event outcomes and mean differences for continuous outcomes, with 95% confidence intervals used for interpretation.
The analysis was stratified by type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus.
Missing standard deviations were reconstructed from p values or confidence intervals when available; Wan’s method or pooled-variance imputation was used in other specified circumstances.
The meta-analysis included 111 articles and 103,922 patients.

canonical_statement: Of 111 included articles, 10 reported SGLT1/2 inhibitor results, 100 reported SGLT2 inhibitor results, and one reported both classes.
Follow-up among included trials ranged from 12 weeks to 4.2 years.

canonical_statement: Cardiovascular outcomes could not be analyzed in T1DM because of insufficient studies.
UACR and serum BUN could not be analyzed, and renal outcomes were not analyzed for T1DM because of insufficient data.
The authors concluded that in T2DM, SGLT1/2 inhibitors were associated with lower myocardial infarction and stroke risk but higher diarrhea and severe hypoglycemia risk than SGLT2 inhibitors.
The authors proposed that SGLT1/2 inhibitors may not confer much additional benefit over SGLT2 inhibitors in T1DM.
Renal composite definitions were inconsistent across included studies, limiting reliability and applicability of that outcome.
The evidence network was highly imbalanced, with 100 SGLT2 inhibitor trials versus 10 SGLT1/2 inhibitor trials.
Myocardial infarction and stroke comparisons relied on only one to two SGLT1/2 inhibitor trials, specifically SCORED and SOLOIST-WHF populations, limiting generalizability to average T2DM patients.
The T2DM severe-hypoglycemia estimate for SGLT1/2 inhibitors was informed by only one SGLT1/2 inhibitor trial.
The meta-analysis used mean aggregate data and did not account for substantial individual-level variation in treatment response.
